[context] But with regard to these Supplementary Instances, although I stated that information was to be derived from them in the absence of instances proper,
as a last resource; yet I wish it to be understood that they are also of great use, even when proper instances are at hand; for the purpose, I mean, of corroborating the information, which the others supply. But I shall treat of them more fully, when I come in due course to speak of the Supports of Induction.
XLIII.
Among Prerogative Instances I will put in the twentieth place Dissecting Instances; which I also call Awakening Instances, but for a different reason. I call them Awakening, because they awaken the understanding; Dissecting, because they dissect nature; for which reason also I sometimes call them Democritean. They are those which remind the understanding of the wonderful and exquisite subtlety of nature, so as to stir it up and awaken it to attention and observation and due investigation. Such, for example, as these following: that a little drop of ink spreads to so many letters or lines; that silver gilt stretches to such a length of gilt wire; that a tiny worm, such as we find in the skin, possesses in itself both spirit and a varied organisation; that a little saffron tinges a whole hogshead of water; that a little civet or musk scents a much larger volume of air; that a little
[context] incense raises such a cloud of smoke;

reference_text:
[context] Sanguification, too, which is entitled the second digestion,
is perfect before the first, or chylification, which takes place in the stomach, is begun. The excrementitious products of the first and second digestions, namely, excrement in the intestines, urine and bile in the urinary and gall bladder, are contemporaneous with the existence of the concocting organs themselves. Lastly, not only is there a soul or vital principle present in the vegetative part, but even before this there is inherent mind, foresight, and understanding, which from the very commencement to the being and perfect formation of the chick, dispose and order and take up all things requisite, moulding them in the new being, with consummate art, into the form and likeness of its parents.

In reference to this subject of family likeness, we may be permitted to inquire as to the reason why the offspring should at one time bear a stronger resemblance to the father, at another to the mother, and, at a third, to progenitors, both maternal and paternal, further removed? particularly in cases where at one bout, and at the same moment, several ova are fecundated. And this too is a remarkable fact, that virtues and vices, marks and moles, and even particular dispositions to disease are transmitted by parents to their offspring; and that while some inherit in this way, all do not. Among our poultry some are courageous, and pugnaciously inclined, and will sooner die than yield and flee from an adversary; their descendants, once or twice removed, however, unless they have come of equally well-bred parents, gradually lose this quality; according to the adage, "the brave are begotten by the brave." In various other species of animals, and particularly in the human family, a certain nobility of race is observed; numerous qualities, in fact, both of mind and body, are derived by hereditary descent.

I have frequently wondered how it should happen that the offspring, mixed in so many particulars of its structure or constitution, with the stamp of both parents so obviously upon it, in so many parts, should still escape all mixture in the organs of generation; that it should so uniformly prove either male or female, so very rarely an hermaphrodite.

Lastly, many things are present before they appear, and some are begun among the very first which are completed among the very last, such as the eyes, the organs of generation, and the beak.

[context] 38. I now come to inquire into the second way of condensing the spirits, namely by cold.
For condensation is the proper work of cold; and it is done without any malignity, or unfriendly quality. The operation, therefore, is safer than by opiates, though somewhat less powerful, if used only at intervals, as opiates are. But then since it may be used in moderation familiarly and as a part of daily diet, it has much more power than opiates to prolong life.
[margin] 39.
Refrigeration of the spirits takes place in three ways; by respiration, by vapours, or by aliments. Of these the first is the best, but mostly out of our power; the second likewise is strong, and yet within our reach; the third is weak and circuitous.

<header>DE ALCHIMIA.</header>

### DE ALCHIMIA.

<margin>Alchimię finis non aurum & argentũ. sed arcana.</margin>
destinauit, penetrent. Ex his colligite, necesse esse, vt ad præscriptum meum procedatur, & minimè ad vestrum. Hic opus est, vt me sectemini, non ego vos. Et licet quidem aduersus me adhuc plura defulminetis: mea tamen nihilominus Monarchia stabit, vestrā cuncte pessum. Frustra de Alchimia tam prolixè non scribo, sed id hoc animo & fine facio, vt ex his propè & solidè cognoscatis, quid in ipsā lateat, & quî intelligi debeat. Nec ex hoc offendi debes, quod ex eā nec aurum, nec argentum prodit: Sed hoc potius accurandum est, vt per eam arcana detegantur, & seductiones seplāsiariorum prodantur, quibus rude vulgus decipitur, dum his pro floreno vno ministrant, quod nummo vno non redimerent. Tam pretiosa eorum arcana sunt.

<margin>Venenū etiam in reb. optimis.</margin>
Quis est, qui inficiari ausit, etiam in rebus optimis venenum latere & inesistere? Fateri id omnes coguntur. Hoc ergò si verum est, ex vobis iam quæro an non à bono & vtili venenum separandum sit? & bonum accipiendum, malum relinquendum? Imò verò, ita oportet. Si itaq; oportet: quæso enarrate mihi, qui id in vestris officinis separetur? Apud vos enim omnia permixta manent. Vt verò simplicitatem vestram tueamini, si conuicti estis ad fatendum, ibi venęnum latere & quò tandem illud abeat, rogamini: tunc nescio quid de correctionibus profertis, quæ venenum exigant & auferant,
<margin>Correctio Medicorum ventilatur.</margin>
veluti Cotonea Scammoneam, post Diagridium, dictum corrigūt. Quid id verò correctionis est? An non manet venenum postea ceu primò? Et tu tamē interim gloriaris, quod correxeris, adeò vt venenum ampliùs non noceat. Id verò quò euasit? 
<margin>Diagridion.</margin>
In Diagridio manet. Id tenta, si sapis: modum excede, & videbis, vbi venenum sit. Nam id haud segniter scies Sic corrigis etiam Turbith, & vocas ipsum Diaturbith. Istiusmodi correctiones vestrę sunt, quæ rusticos decerent, & caballis propinandæ essent. Excedēndo modum periculum fac, & dosin auge: videris an venenum non sensurus sis. 
<margin>Corrigo Medicu quid</margin>
*Corrigere est correctum sumere.* Qui malitiosus est, & peccauit: is si plectitur, correctio non extēditur longius, quàm voluntas durat eius, qui plexus est. Tales hæ quoque correctiones sunt, penes ipsas fitum est, non penes te. Iam verò hoc casu nihil considerandum Medico est ampliùs, quàm vt venenum dematur. Id per separationem fieri oportet: Vt, exempli gratia: serpens venenosus est: & tamen in cibum adoptatur. Si ipsi venenu demis, comedas nullā noxā. Idem de rebus cæteris vniuersis æquè intelligendum est, nimirùm simili separatione opus esse. Eā nondum factā, operationis tuæ securus esse non possis: nisi forte fiat, vt vices tuas natura suppleat, aut cœli maior benignitas faueat. In arte etenim tuā præsidij nihil superfuerit.

Iam ergò tandem verum illud fundamentum si oportet, quod venenum aufert, qualiter id Alchimia præstat. Hoc enim ita fieri necesse est, vt, si Mars in Sole sit, Mars dematur, & si Saturnus in Venere versetur, is ab eā separetur. Quot enim ascendentes & impressiones in rebus naturæ sunt, tot etiam corpora in illis existunt. Quæ verò corpora contraria sunt, eorum omninò aliquod demi & auferri opus est, vt hoc pacto omnis contrarietas tollatur, & à bono malum, quod quæris, adimatur.
<margin>Ignis omnia perficit.</margin>
Ut aurum ad nihil vtile est, nisi priùs in ignem coniiciatur: sic multò minùs vtilis Medicina est, quæ per ignem non transit. Per ignem enim necesse est omnia transire in generationem alteram, quā homini conducere & opitulari debet. Et hoc non meritò probum fundamentum cuiuslibet Medici censeri debeat? Nec enim Medicus venena, verū arcana adhibere debet. 
<margin>Officinę reprehend.</margin>
Omnes autem illæ officinales præparationes, quotquot earum sunt, isti doctrinæ ne quidem literulam conferunt: sed in corrigendo simpliciter occupantur, velut; si canis in conclaui pepedit, & fœtor ille aut trochiscis & thymiamate, aut ligno iuniperino sopiatur: an non quęso fœtor tam postea, quàm antea in cōclaui remanet? Et licet quidem olfactu non percipiatur: an ideò cuipiam dicere liceat, fœtor separatus est, nec restat ampliùs? Imò adest, sed correctus suffitu. Sic ergò suffitus & pedor nares vnà ingrediuntur. Huiusmodiquoque sunt correctiones Pharmacopœorum, qui saccharo obtundunt Aleopaticum, vt sic nullam noxam infligat. Ita saccharū & mel ipsorum magisteriū est. Sic gentianā etiā corrigūt theriacam. An verò hæc non asininæ inscitiæ opera sint? Ipsi tamen se principum Medicos iactant & venditant. Quis verò ita stupidus est, vt hæc nihili esse, non illicò olfaciat? De remediis suis quid quæso iactare possunt aliud, quàm vt dicant, *Hoc Electuarium suaue est, ex aromatis, saccharo, melléque*

<vocab>Alchimia, Mars, Saturnus, Scammoneam, Diagridium, Turbith, Medicus, Electuarium, seplasiariorum</vocab>
reference_text:
[context] Truly, indeed, they are, in order that such errors may be avoided, and patients may advance to those sure arcana which God has designed for their use and requirement.
You will gather from hence how necessary it is to act on my prescription rather than on yours. In this respect you have to follow me, not I to follow you. Though you fulminate ever so much against me, nevertheless, my monarchy shall stand, while yours goes to destruction. It is not in vain that I write at such length concerning Alchemy, but I do it with this purpose and for this end, that you may well and surely know what is latent therein, and how it should be understood. Nor should you be offended hereby because you get no gold or silver by it. Rather its result should be that by means thereof arcana shall be unveiled, and the seductions of the ointment-sellers shall be brought to light, since by these the ignorant folk are deceived, while they sell them for a florin what they would not buy back for a penny. So precious, in this sense, are their secrets!

Who will deny that even in the very best things a poison may lie hid? All must acknowledge this. And if this be true, I would now ask you whether it is not right that the poison should be separated from what is good and useful, that the good should be taken and the evil left. Such should certainly be the case. If so, tell me how it is separated in your surgeries. With you all these elements remain mixed. See your own simplicity, then, if you are forced to confess that a poison lies hid, and are asked how it is to be got rid of. Then you bring forward I know not what correctives, which shall drive out and take away the poison. Comfrey, for example, they use to correct scammony, which is then called diagridium. But what kind of a corrective is this? Does not the poison remain afterwards as before? And yet you boast that you have so corrected it that the poison no longer harms. Whither has it gone? It remains in the diagridium. Try it, if you are wise. Exceed the proper dose, and you will soon see where the poison is. You will not be long in finding out. So you correct turbith also, and then call it diaturbith. These are your methods of correction, fit only for clowns, and useful to drench horses with! Risk an excessive dose; you will see whether you do not feel the poison. To correct is to take that which has been corrected. A criminal who has broken the law is punished; but his correction is not extended farther than the free will of the culprit lasts. Such are your corrections. The power is in them, not in you. In such a case, all the physician thinks of is how to eliminate the poison. This must be done by separation. For example, a serpent is venomous, and yet it is used for food. If you take away the poison you can eat the flesh without injury. And so it is with all other substances; only a similar separation is absolutely necessary. If this is not brought about, you cannot be sure of your work, unless, indeed, it come to pass that Nature supplies your place, or some special interposition of providence favours you. You have no protection in your art. If a sure foundation be necessary for the extraction of the poison, that is afforded by Alchemy. It must be so arranged that if there be Mars in Sol, Mars must be taken away; or Saturn in Venus, the Saturn must be separated from the Venus. As many ascendants and impressions as there are in natural substances, so many bodies are there in them. But when the bodies are contrary, it is absolutely necessary that one of them should be taken away and removed, so that in this way all contrariety should be eliminated, and so the evil which you are searching for should be separated from the good. As gold is useless except it shall first have passed through the fire, so medicine is much less useful unless it, too, shall have passed through the fire. It is necessary that everything which is to benefit man shall have passed by fire to a second birth. Should not this, then, be deemed the right fundamental principle of every physician? A physician should exhibit not poisons, but arcana. But all the preparations of your surgeries, how many soever they be, do not contribute the smallest tittle of learning. They are employed simply in correcting, which is just as if a dog should break wind in a room and you should kill the stink with fumigations and juniper wood; but does not the smell remain in the room as much after as before that process? Although the smell is not perceptible by the olfactory organs, could anybody say that the stink was separated and no longer remained? It is there, though corrected by the fumigation. The stink and the fumigation enter the nose together. Of such a sort also are the corrections of the drug-vendors who disguise aloepaticum with sugar, that it may not offend the palate. The sugar and the honey form a magistery in this case. So, too, they correct theriacum with gentian. Are not all these operations instances of asinine ignorance? And yet these people boast themselves the physicians of princes, and sell their skill for money! Yet who is so dense as not to scent the fact forthwith that all this is worthless? What else can they trumpet forth about their remedies beyond saying "This electuary is sweet, being compounded of spices, sugar, honey,
[context] and other condiments, and is held in very great esteem?"

### ON ALCHEMY.

<margin>The goal of alchemy is not gold and silver, but arcana <gloss>mysteries/secret remedies</gloss>.</margin>
It has ordained that they should penetrate. From these things, conclude that it is necessary to proceed according to my prescription, and not at all to yours. Here, it is necessary that you follow me, not I you. And although you may yet thunder many things against me, my Monarchy shall nevertheless stand, while yours will perish entirely. I do not write so prolixly about Alchemy in vain, but I do so with this intent and purpose: that from these things you may know closely and solidly what lies hidden within it, and how it ought to be understood. Nor should you be offended by the fact that neither gold nor silver comes forth from it. But rather, this must be sought: that through it, the arcana may be discovered, and the deceptions of the apothecaries <gloss>merchants of perfumes and drugs</gloss> be exposed, by which the crude masses are deceived, while they serve them for one florin what would not be redeemed for a single coin. So precious are their arcana.

<margin>Poison exists even in the best things.</margin>
Who is there who dares to deny that poison lies hidden and exists even in the best things? All are compelled to confess this. If this is true, then I ask you now: should poison not be separated from the good and the useful, and the good accepted while the evil is left behind? Indeed, it must be so. If, therefore, it is necessary, I ask you to explain to me: how is this separated in your workshops? For with you, everything remains mixed. But in order to defend your simplicity, if you are convicted of confessing that poison lies hidden there, and you are asked where it finally goes, you then bring up some nonsense about "corrections" that demand and remove the poison,
<margin>The correction of physicians is examined.</margin>
just as they correct Quince with Scammony, or later with Diagridium <gloss>a preparation of scammony</gloss>. What kind of correction is that, truly? Does the poison not remain afterwards just as it was at first? And yet, in the meantime, you boast that you have corrected it, so that the poison no longer harms. But where has it gone?
<margin>Diagridion.</margin>
It remains in the Diagridium. Try this, if you are wise: exceed the measure, and you will see where the poison is. For you will know this quite promptly. Thus you also correct Turbith <gloss>a purgative root</gloss>, and call it Diaturbith. Such are your corrections, which would befit rustics and should be given to horses. Make a trial by exceeding the measure, and increase the dose: you will see if you do not feel the poison.
<margin>What it is to correct a medicine.</margin>
*To correct is to take the corrected.* If a man is wicked and has sinned, if he is punished, the correction does not extend further than the will of the one who is punished lasts. Such are these corrections; they depend on the things themselves, not on you. Now, in this case, a physician must consider nothing more than that the poison should be removed. This must be done through separation. As, for example: a serpent is poisonous, and yet it is adopted into food. If you remove the poison from it, you may eat it without any harm. The same must be understood equally of all other things; namely, that there is a need for a similar separation. That not yet done, you cannot be secure in your operation, unless by chance it happens that nature supplies your shortcomings, or a greater kindness of the heavens favors you. For in your art, nothing of assistance will remain.

Now, therefore, if that true foundation is necessary which removes the poison, how does Alchemy achieve this? For it must be done in such a way that, if Mars <gloss>iron</gloss> is in the Sun <gloss>gold</gloss>, Mars should be removed, and if Saturn <gloss>lead</gloss> dwells in Venus <gloss>copper</gloss>, it should be separated from it. For as many ascendants and impressions as there are in the things of nature, so many bodies exist within them. But as for those bodies which are contrary, it is necessary that some part of them be entirely removed and taken away, so that in this way all contrariety may be lifted, and the evil which you seek may be removed from the good.
<margin>Fire perfects all things.</margin>
Just as gold is useless for anything unless it is first thrown into the fire, so much less useful is a medicine which does not pass through the fire. For it is necessary for all things to pass through the fire into a second generation, which ought to be beneficial and helpful to man. And should this not deservedly be considered the sound foundation of any physician? For a physician ought not to apply poisons, but true arcana.
<margin>Workshops criticized.</margin>
However, all those workshop preparations, as many as they are, do not contribute even a letter to this doctrine; rather, they are occupied simply with correcting, just as if a dog should pass gas in a room, and that stench is quieted either by troches <gloss>medicinal lozenges</gloss> and incense, or by juniper wood: does the stench not remain in the room afterwards just as much as before? And although it may not be perceived by the sense of smell, is it therefore permitted for anyone to say that the stench has been separated and no longer remains? Indeed, it is present, but masked by smoke. Thus, the smoke and the stench enter the nostrils together. Such are also the corrections of the apothecaries, who dull the Aleopatic <note>a purgative medicine; original: "Aleopaticum"</note> with sugar, so that it may inflict no harm. Thus, sugar and honey are their masteries. Thus they even correct gentian with theriac <gloss>a medicinal treacle</gloss>. But are these not works of asinine ignorance? Yet they boast and sell themselves as the chief of physicians. But who is so stupid as not to smell immediately that these are worth nothing? Of their remedies, what I ask can they boast other than to say, *This electuary is sweet, made from aromatics, sugar, and honey*

Tertius ar. utrum magis uniuersalia sint priora in nostra cognitione intellectuali.

Dtertium sic, proceditur. Ut quod magis uniuersalia non sint priora in nostra cognitione in-tellectuali: quia ea que sunt priora notiora secundum naturam sunt posteriora et minus nota secundum nos, sed uniuersalia sunt priora secundum naturam nostri intellectus. Preterea composita sunt priora quo ad nos et simplicia. sed uniuersalia sunt priora cioza: sunt posterius nota quo ad nos. Preterea philosophus dicit in primo physicorum diffinitus prius cadit in cognitione nostra et partes diffinitionis minus uniuersali: sicut animal est pars diffinitionis hominis: et uniuersalia sunt posterius nota quo ad nos. Preterea effectus euenimus et casu et principia. sed uniuersalia sunt posterius nota quo ad nos. Sed si est quod or in in primo physicorum ex libris in singularia os deuenire. Respondeo dicendum quod in cognitione nostri intellectus duo os considerare. primo quidem quod cognitio intellectiua aliquo modo a sensitiua primordium sumit. et quia sensus est singularium in intellectus et uniuersalius: necesse est quod cognitio singularium quo ad nos sit uniuersalius cognitio. secundo os considerare quod intellectus nr de potentia ad actum procedit. et quod procedit de potentia in actum prius peruenit ad actum incompletum qui est medius inter potentia et actus et actus perfectus. aut perfectus ad quem peruenit intellectus est scia completa per quas distincte et determinate res cognoscuntur: actus et incompletus est scia imperfecta per quam sciuntur res indistincte sub quadaz confusione. quod enim sic cognoscitur tam quod cognoscitur in actu et quodammodo in potentia. ut in primo physicorum dicit in primo physicorum: sit primum nobis manifesta et certa confusa magis. posterius autem cognoscimus distinguendo distincte principia et elementa. manifestum est autem quod cognoscere aliquid in quo plura continentur sine hoc quod habeatur propria notitia uniuscuiusque eorum que continentur in illo est cognoscere aliquid sub confusione quadam. sic autem potest cognosci tam totum uel in quo partes continentur in potentia et totum integrale: utrumque enim totum potest cognosci in quadam confusione sine hoc quod partes distincte cognoscantur. cognoscere autem distincte id quod continetur in toto uel est habere cognitionem de re minus communi: sicut cognoscere animal indistincte et cognoscere animal in quo cum est rationale aut irrationale quod est cognoscere homine ut leonem. prius igitur occurrit intellectui nostro cognoscere animal et cognoscere homine. et cadere rone si comparem quodcumque magis uel ad minus ut sensus exit de potentia in actu sic intellectus: id et ordo

Ad primum et quod per duplex potest os siderari. uno et quod per os siderat sic et intentio ueritatis. et cum intentio ueritatis et uerum et idem beat habitudinem ad multa. pueniat et abstractio intellectus os finis hic modo dum uere sit posterius. in in primo de anima et quantitatem uniuersale aut nihil est aut posterius est: sed et plus tonem et posuit uniuersalia suba: et in hanc confide rationem uerem est: plus quia particularia et cum non sunt nisi per participationem uniuersalius sub sistentium que dicitur idee. alio modo potest conside rari et tum ad ipsam naturam. animalitatis et uel bu manitatis et put inuenitur in particularibus. et sic est duplex et ordo nature. unus fecundum uiam generationis et tempus cum uiam ea que sunt im perfecta et in potentia sunt priora. et hoc modo magis et est pus et in nam quod apparet manifeste in generatione bo minis et aialis. naz prius generatur animal bo: ut et or in in libro de generatione animalium. alius et ordo et perfectionis siue intentionis nature sicut actus simpliciter et pus et in naturam et quod per et pfectum per et quod ipse fecrum: et p hoc modo minus et est pus et in nam naz et bo aial. nature in intentio non sitit in generatione aia lis: et intendit generare hominem. THIRD ARTICLE [I, Q. 85, Art. 3]

Whether the More Universal Is First in Our Intellectual Cognition?

Objection 1: It would seem that the more universal is not first in our intellectual cognition. For what is first and more known in its own nature, is secondarily and less known in relation to ourselves. But universals come first as regards their nature, because "that is first which does not involve the existence of its correlative" (Categor. ix). Therefore the universals are secondarily known as regards our intellect.

Obj. 2: Further, the composition precedes the simple in relation to us. But universals are the more simple. Therefore they are known secondarily by us.

Obj. 3: Further, the Philosopher says (Phys. i, 1), that the object defined comes in our knowledge before the parts of its definition. But the more universal is part of the definition of the less universal, as "animal" is part of the definition of "man." Therefore the universals are secondarily known by us.

Obj. 4: Further, we know causes and principles by their effects. But universals are principles. Therefore universals are secondarily known by us.

On the contrary, "We must proceed from the universal to the singular and individual" (Phys. i, 1)

I answer that, In our knowledge there are two things to be considered. First, that intellectual knowledge in some degree arises from sensible knowledge: and, because sense has singular and individual things for its object, and intellect has the universal for its object, it follows that our knowledge of the former comes before our knowledge of the latter. Secondly, we must consider that our intellect proceeds from a state of potentiality to a state of actuality; and every power thus proceeding from potentiality to actuality comes first to an incomplete act, which is the medium between potentiality and actuality, before accomplishing the perfect act. The perfect act of the intellect is complete knowledge, when the object is distinctly and determinately known; whereas the incomplete act is imperfect knowledge, when the object is known indistinctly, and as it were confusedly. A thing thus imperfectly known, is known partly in act and partly in potentiality, and hence the Philosopher says (Phys. i, 1), that "what is manifest and certain is known to us at first confusedly; afterwards we know it by distinguishing its principles and elements." Now it is evident that to know an object that comprises many things, without proper knowledge of each thing contained in it, is to know that thing confusedly. In this way we can have knowledge not only of the universal whole, which contains parts potentially, but also of the integral whole; for each whole can be known confusedly, without its parts being known. But to know distinctly what is contained in the universal whole is to know the less common, as to "animal" indistinctly is to know it as "animal"; whereas to know "animal" distinctly is know it as "rational" or "irrational animal," that is, to know a man or a lion: therefore our intellect knows "animal" before it knows man; and the same reason holds in comparing any more universal idea with the less universal.

Moreover, as sense, like the intellect, proceeds from potentiality to act, the same order of knowledge appears in the senses. For by sense we judge of the more common before the less common, in reference both to place and time; in reference to place, when a thing is seen afar off it is seen to be a body before it is seen to be an animal; and to be an animal before it is seen to be a man, and to be a man before it seen to be Socrates or Plato; and the same is true as regards time, for a child can distinguish man from not man before he distinguishes this man from that, and therefore "children at first call men fathers, and later on distinguish each one from the others" (Phys. i, 1). The reason of this is clear: because he who knows a thing indistinctly is in a state of potentiality as regards its principle of distinction; as he who knows genus is in a state of potentiality as regards "difference." Thus it is evident that indistinct knowledge is midway between potentiality and act.

We must therefore conclude that knowledge of the singular and individual is prior, as regards us, to the knowledge of the universal; as sensible knowledge is prior to intellectual knowledge. But in both sense and intellect the knowledge of the more common precedes the knowledge of the less common.

Reply Obj. 1: The universal can be considered in two ways. First, the universal nature may be considered together with the intention of universality. And since the intention of universality--viz. the relation of one and the same to many--is due to intellectual abstraction, the universal thus considered is a secondary consideration. Hence it is said (De Anima i, 1) that the "universal animal is either nothing or something secondary." But according to Plato, who held that universals are subsistent, the universal considered thus would be prior to the particular, for the latter, according to him, are mere participations of the subsistent universals which he called ideas.

Secondly, the universal can be considered in the nature itself--for instance, animality or humanity as existing in the individual. And thus we must distinguish two orders of nature: one, by way of generation and time; and thus the imperfect and the potential come first. In this way the more common comes first in the order of nature; as appears clearly in the generation of man and animal; for "the animal is generated before man," as the Philosopher says (De Gener. Animal ii, 3). The other order is the order of perfection or of the intention of nature: for instance, act considered absolutely is naturally prior to potentiality, and the perfect to the imperfect: thus the less common comes naturally before the more common; as man comes before animal. For the intention of nature does not stop at the generation of animal but goes on to the generation of man.

Reply Obj. 2: The more common universal may be compared to the less common, as the whole, and as the part. As the whole, considering that in the more universal is potentially contained not only the less universal, but also other things, as in "animal" is contained not only "man" but also "horse." As part, considering that the less common contains in its idea not only the more common, but also more; as "man" contains not only "animal" but also "rational." Therefore "animal" in itself comes into our knowledge before "man"; but "man" comes before "animal" considered as part of the same idea.

Reply Obj. 3: A part can be known in two ways. First, absolutely considered in itself; and thus nothing prevents the parts being known before the whole, as stones are known before a house is known. Secondly as belonging to a certain whole; and thus we must needs know the whole before its parts. For we know a house vaguely before we know its different parts. So likewise principles of definition are known before the thing defined is known; otherwise the thing defined would not be known at all. But as parts
[context] of the definition they are known after. For we know man vaguely as man before we know how to distinguish all that belongs to human nature.

Question

<column-break/>

Article 3. Whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition.

Regarding the third point, the following procedure is taken. It seems that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition, because those things which are prior according to nature are posterior and less known to us; but universals are prior according to the nature of our intellect. Furthermore, composite things are prior relative to us, while simple things are posterior. But universals are prior, and thus they are posterior in our knowledge relative to us. Furthermore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the *Physics* that the defined falls into our cognition prior to the parts of the definition, and those parts are less universal, just as "animal" is a part of the definition of "man," and universals are known later relative to us. Furthermore, effects are known to us, and principles are known later relative to us. But there is that which the Philosopher says in the first book of the *Physics* regarding coming to know singulars from universals. 

I answer that it must be said that two things must be considered in the cognition of our intellect. First, intellectual cognition takes its origin in some way from sensory cognition. And because sense is of singulars, and the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars be prior to the cognition of universals relative to us. Second, it must be considered that our intellect proceeds from potency to act. And what proceeds from potency to act arrives first at an incomplete act, which is the medium between potency and complete act. The perfect act to which the intellect arrives is complete science, through which things are known distinctly and determinately. The incomplete act is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is known in this way is known as something that is in act and in a certain way in potency. As it is said in the first book of the *Physics*, things are first manifest and certain to us in a more confused way; later, however, we know things by distinguishing the principles and elements distinctly. It is manifest, however, that to know something in which many things are contained without having proper knowledge of each of the things contained therein is to know something under a certain confusion. Thus, both the whole, in which parts are contained in potency, and the integral whole can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being known distinctly. To know distinctly that which is contained in the whole, however, is to have knowledge of a less common thing, just as to know "animal" indistinctly, and to know the "animal" in which it is rational or irrational, which is to know "man" or "lion." Therefore, it occurs to our intellect to know "animal" prior to knowing "man." And if I compare it to whatever is more or less universal, just as sense exits from potency into act, so does the intellect; and this order

<column-break/>

of cognition appears in sense. For in sense, a person distinguishes more remote things and, when something is known, it is known more remotely, for example, "body," then "animal," and then "man." And a person observes "body" first, then "animal," then "man." Or it pleases <note>the observation</note> that it is evident that a child, from the beginning, distinguishes "man" from "not-man," and in the beginning, children call all men "fathers." Later, however, they determine each one, as the Philosopher says in the first book of the *Physics*: things are manifest, and one who knows something still indistinctly and in potency knows it as a fiction and a principle, and thus he knows genera and is able to know species. And thus, by itself, indistinct cognition is the medium between potency and act. And thus the cognition of singulars is prior relative to us, as is the cognition of universals, both sensory cognition and intellectual cognition. If, therefore, there is both sense and intellect, the cognition of the more universal is prior, and the cognition of the lesser and more common is also prior. 

To the first, it must be said that this can be considered in two ways. In one way, it can be considered according to the intention of truth. And since the intention of truth and the truth itself have a relationship to many things, and the abstraction of the intellect reaches this end, in this way the universal is posterior. As it is said in the first book of *De Anima*, the universal is either nothing or it is posterior. But because Plato <note>alluding to Plato's Theory of Forms</note> posited universals as substances, and in this consideration he is wrong, because particulars are nothing except through the participation of the more universal subsisting things, which are called *ideas*. In another way, it can be considered according to the nature itself of animality or humanity, as it is found in particulars. And thus there is a double order of nature. One is according to the way of generation and time, when those things that are imperfect and in potency are prior. And in this way, the more universal is prior in nature, which appears manifestly in the generation of man and animal. For "animal" is generated prior to "man," as the Philosopher says in the book *De Generatione Animalium*. The other is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, just as an act is simply prior in nature, because that which is perfect is prior to that which is imperfect. And in this way, the less universal is prior in nature, for nature does not rest in the generation of "animal," but it intends to generate "man." 

To the second, it must be said that the more universal is compared to the less universal as a whole. And through the whole, which is made more universal, it is not only "animal" but also "man" and "horse," just as the less universal is contained not only in the more universal but also in others, like "man" not only in "animal," but also in "rational." Thus, therefore, "animal" considered in itself is prior in our cognition to "man." If "man" is prior in our cognition, then "animal" is so through its reason. 

To the third, it must be said that something can be known in two ways. In one way, absolutely, according to what it is in itself, and thus nothing is known <unclear>partially</unclear>. In another way, when it is part of this whole, such as stones, it is necessary that we know the whole prior to the parts. For we know the house in a certain confused way. Thus, therefore, it must be said that the definition, to be considered absolutely, is prior to the thing defined. Otherwise, the defined would not be made known through the parts of the definition, but rather the parts are what they are.

<summary>This passage examines the priority of universal versus singular knowledge in the human intellect, distinguishing between the order of sensory generation and the order of formal perfection.</summary>
<keywords>Intellect, Universals, Singulars, Potency, Act, Sensory Cognition, Thomas Aquinas, Physics, Aristotle, Generation, Perfection</keywords>

Question

<column-break/>

Article 3. Whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition.

Regarding the third point, it is argued as follows. It seems that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition, because things that are prior by nature are posterior and less known to us; but universals are prior by nature of our intellect. Furthermore, composite things are prior to us compared to simple things, but universals are prior to <unclear>singulars</unclear> and are posterior in terms of being known to us. Furthermore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the *Physics* that the defined falls into our cognition prior to the parts of the definition, and those parts are less universal; for instance, "animal" is a part of the definition of "man," yet universals are known later to us. Furthermore, we encounter effects and their causes by chance, but universals are known later to us. However, it is stated in the first book of the *Physics* that we must proceed from the universal to the singular. I respond that in the cognition of our intellect, two things must be considered. First, intellectual cognition takes its beginning in some way from sensory cognition. And because sense is of singulars, while the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars be prior to us than the cognition of universals. Second, we must consider that our intellect proceeds from potency to act. And what proceeds from potency to act arrives first at an incomplete act, which is intermediate between potency and perfect act. The perfect act to which the intellect arrives is complete science, through which things are known distinctly and determinately; the incomplete act is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is known in this way is known as if in act and in a certain way in potency. As it is said in the first book of the *Physics*: things are initially manifest and certain to us in a more confused way; later, however, we come to know by distinguishing principles and elements distinctly. It is manifest, however, that to know something in which many things are contained, without having proper knowledge of each of those things contained within it, is to know something in a certain confusion. In this way, both the whole in which the parts are contained potentially and the integral whole can be known; for both wholes can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being known distinctly. However, to know distinctly that which is contained in the whole is to have knowledge of a less common thing; as, for instance, knowing "animal" indistinctly, and knowing the animal in which there is rationality or irrationality, which is to know "man" or "lion." Therefore, it occurs first to our intellect to know "animal" and to know "man," and this follows the order of reason, if I compare whatever is more or less universal, just as sense departs from potency into act, so does the intellect; this is the order

<column-break/>

of cognition appearing in sense. For in sense, we distinguish more initially, and when a thing is known more remotely, <unclear>it is perceived</unclear> as a being, then as a body, then as a living being; and one perceives it as a living being, then as a being, then as a good, and prior to that as a being and as a substance. Or it pleases and it is clear that a child from the beginning first distinguishes a "good" from a "non-good"; and children at the beginning call all men "fathers." Later, however, he determines each one, as is said in the first book of the *Physics*: he knows something indistinctly still and in potency, or he knows the genus and the principle, and so he knows the species and can eventually know the differences. And thus, in itself, indistinct cognition is intermediate between potency and act. And thus, the cognition of singulars is prior to us, and the cognition of universals is sensory cognition and intellectual cognition. If we consider both sense and intellect, the cognition of the more universal is prior to the cognition of the less common. Regarding the first point, that which is considered through a twofold method can be considered in two ways. One way is through the intention of truth. And since the intention of truth and the true itself have a relationship to many things, the abstraction of the intellect arrives at the end; in this way, the universal is posterior. As in the first book *On the Soul*, the universal either is nothing or is posterior; but <unclear>Plato</unclear> posited universals as substances; and in this consideration, it is true, because particulars are not except by the participation of those subsisting universals which are called "ideas." In another way, it can be considered with respect to the nature itself of animality or humanity, as it is found in particulars. And thus there is a twofold order of nature. One is according to the path of generation and time, in which those things which are imperfect and in potency are prior. And in this way, the less universal is prior in nature, as appears manifestly in the generation of a man and an animal; for the animal is generated prior to the man, as is said in the book *On the Generation of Animals*. The other is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, such as act, which is simply prior to nature, because what is perfect is prior to that which is being perfected; and in this way, the more universal is prior in nature, for nature does not rest in the generation of an animal, but intends to generate a human being. Regarding the second point, the more universal is compared to the less universal as the whole, and because the whole that is more universal contains not only the species, such as man and horse, but also the less universal, and contains in the future not only the more universal but also others, as "man" not only contains "animal" but also "rational." Thus, therefore, "animal" considered in itself is prior in our cognition to "man," if "man" is prior in our cognition and "animal" is so through its reason. Regarding the third point, it must be said that something can be known in two ways. In one way, absolutely, according to what it is in itself, and thus nothing is known prior to the house. In another way, as it is a part of this whole, and just as with stones, it is necessary that we know the whole prior to the parts. For we know the house first in a certain confused way. Thus, therefore, it must be said that the definition considered absolutely is prior to the defined. Otherwise, the defined would not be notified through it, but rather through those things that are parts.

<summary>This page explores the cognitive relationship between universal concepts and singular particulars, arguing that while sensory experience begins with the singular, intellectual development proceeds from confused, universal awareness toward distinct, specific knowledge.</summary>
<keywords>Intellect, Universals, Singulars, Cognition, Sensory Perception, Potentiality, Actuality, Definition, Nature of Generation, Aristotle</keywords>

Questio

<column-break/>

The third article: whether the more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition.

Regarding the third point, the procedure is as follows. It seems that the more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition, because those things which are prior according to nature are posterior and less known to us, but the universals are prior according to nature. Furthermore, composite things are prior with respect to us, and simple things are posterior. But the universals are prior; therefore, they are known later with respect to us. Furthermore, the Philosopher says in the first book of the *Physics* that a definition falls into our cognition before its parts, and the parts of a definition are less universal, just as "animal" is a part of the definition of "human"; and the universals are known later with respect to us. Furthermore, we arrive at effects and principles by chance. But the universals are known later with respect to us. But if it is that, as is said in the first book of the *Physics*, from the books into singulars we must arrive. I answer that it must be said that in the cognition of our intellect, two things must be considered. First, that intellectual cognition in some way takes its origin from sensory cognition. And because sensation is of singulars, and the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars be prior with respect to us than the cognition of universals. Second, it must be considered that our intellect proceeds from potency to act. And that which proceeds from potency to act arrives first at an incomplete act, which is the midpoint between potency and perfect act. But the perfect act to which the intellect arrives is complete science, through which things are known distinctly and determinately; the incomplete act is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is known in this way is both known in act and in a certain way in potency. As is said in the first book of the *Physics*: the first things manifest and certain to us are rather confused; afterwards, we know by distinguishing distinctly the principles and elements. It is manifest, however, that to know something in which many things are contained without having the proper knowledge of each of the things contained in it, is to know something under a certain confusion. In this way, however, both a whole in which parts are contained in potency and an integral whole can be known; for each whole can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being known distinctly. However, to know distinctly that which is contained in the whole is to have cognition of a less common thing: just as to know "animal" indistinctly, and to know the "animal" in which there is rational or irrational, which is to know a "human" or a "lion." It occurs to our intellect, therefore, to know "animal" before knowing "human." And if I compare any thing, whether more or less, as sensation exits from potency into act, so does the intellect: that is the order.

<column-break/>

The order of cognition appears in sensation. For more in sensation we distinguish more, and when the less is known, it is further away through <unclear>it is, it is bodily</unclear>, and <unclear>it is</unclear> and animal, and more is known, being animal, and <unclear>it is</unclear> and the good, and prior the good and <unclear>Socrates</unclear>. Or it pleases and it is evident that a child from the beginning distinguishes the good and from the good; and children from the beginning call all men "father." Afterwards, however, one terminates in each one, as is said in the first book of the *Physics*: since it is manifest that one knows something indistinctly still and in potency, or one knows it as a fiction and a principle; thus it is, and one knows kinds, and can know things. And thus, by itself, indistinct cognition is the midpoint between potency and act. And that the cognition of singulars is prior with respect to us, and the cognition of universals is sensory cognition and intellectual cognition. If it is both sense and with intellect, the cognition of the greater is prior to the cognition of the lesser and the common. To the first, it is said that it can be considered in a twofold way. One way is that it is considered as the intention of truth. And since the intention of truth and the true and the same have a relationship to many things, and the abstraction of the intellect reaches this end, in this way the universal is posterior. As in the first book *On the Soul*, the universal is either nothing or it is posterior; but <unclear>it is more</unclear> and he placed the universals as substances, and in this opinion, it is true, more because the particulars are not except through participation in the universals that are subsistent, which are called ideas. In another way, it can be considered with respect to the nature itself of animality and of humanity, as it is found in particulars. And thus there is a twofold order of nature. One is according to the way of generation and time, when those things which are imperfect and in potency are prior. And in this way, the greater is prior, as appears manifestly in the generation of a human and an animal. For prior is generated the animal, then the human, as is said in the book *On the Generation of Animals*. Another is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, such as act, which is simply prior and in nature, and that which is perfect is prior to that which is being perfected; and in this way, the lesser is prior and is in nature, for the animal and the human. The intention of nature does not rest in the generation of the animal, but intends to generate the human. To the second, the more universal is compared to the less universal as a whole, and through the whole, it becomes more universal, not only the good or the human or the horse, as it can, and the less universal is contained in the future not only the greater, but also others, as human in not only animal but rational. Thus, therefore, animal considered in itself is prior in our cognition, and human, if human is prior in our cognition, and animal, thus through its reason. To the third, it must be said that something can be known in two ways. In one way, absolutely, according to what it is in itself, and thus nothing is a house. In another way, when it is a part of this whole, and stones, it is necessary that we know the whole before the parts. For we know the house first in a confused way; thus, therefore, it must be said that the definition to be considered absolutely is made prior to us and defined. Otherwise, the defined would not be notified through those things, but rather those which are the parts.

<summary>This page discusses whether universal concepts are known prior to singulars in intellectual cognition, concluding that while universals are prior in nature, cognition proceeds from confused, imperfect understanding to distinct, perfect knowledge.</summary>
<keywords>Intellectual cognition, universals, singulars, potency, act, Aristotelian physics, definition, sensory knowledge</keywords>

fatim. <term>EV.</term> Quas aves heic video? <term>CA.</term> Est collegii patriarcha. Ne subducito te; jam potarunt; accumbe paullisper; illo digresso fabulabimur nostro more. <term>EV.</term> Age obtestabor tibi, quæ mihi noluisti. Nunc soli sumus, narra totam fabulam, malim enim ex te cognoscere. <term>CA.</term> Ex tot amicis, quos putabam pere plurimum, nunc sentio nullum fuisse, qui mihi prudentius ac senilius consilium dederit, quam tu omnium natu minimus. <term>EV.</term> Sed quo modo expugnasti parentum affectum? <term>CA.</term> Primum improbis hortatibus monachorum, ac monacharum: deinde etiam meis: precibus ac blandimentis labefactus est matris animus: pater nullo pacto quibat perpelli. Tandem omnibus admotis machinis & hic victus & oppressus est potius, quam assensit. Factum est inter pocula: minitabantur horribile malum exitium, si Christo suam sponsam denegaret. <term>EV.</term> O improbitatem stolidorum! Quid fit deinde? <term>CA.</term> Servor triduo domi clam: interim semper aderant mulieres aliquot ejus collegii, quas illi Conversas vocant, hortatibus addentes animum, ut persisterem in sancto proposito, ac solicite caventes, ne qua cognatarum, aut sodalium adiret me, quæ mentem videretur mutatura. Interim adornabantur vestes, aliaque quæ ad convivium attinebant. <term>EV.</term> Tibi quid interim erat animi? Num vacillabas? <term>CA.</term> Non, sed passa sum quiddam tam horrendum, ut malim emori decies, quam iterum perpeti. <term>EV.</term> Quæso, quid istuc est? <term>CA.</term> Non possum effari. <term>EV.</term> Quod mihi dixeris, amico tuo dixeris. <term>CA.</term> Promittis silentium? <term>EV.</term> Id præstaturus eram, etiam si nihil fuisses stipulata. Quasi vero me nondum noris.

[context] Ca. Why in such Haste? Stay a little; pray stay. I'll put on my better Looks, and we'll be merry together.
Eu. What Sort of Cattle have we got here?
Ca. 'Tis the Patriarch of the College: Don't go away, they have had their Dose of Fuddle: Stay but a little While, and as soon as he is gone, we will discourse as we use to do.
Eu. Well, I'll be so good natur'd as to hearken to you, though you would not to me. Now we are alone, you must tell me the whole Story, I would fain have it from your Mouth.
Ca. Now I have found by Experience, of all my Friends, which I took to be very wise Men too, that no Body gave more wise and grave Advice than you, that are the youngest of 'em all.
Eu. Tell me, how did you get your Parents Consent at last?
Ca. First, by the restless Sollicitations of the Monks and Nuns, and then by my own Importunities and Tears, my Mother was at length brought over; but my Father stood out stiffly still: But at last being ply'd by several Engines, he was prevail'd upon to yield; but yet, rather like one that was forced, than that consented. The Matter was concluded in their Cups, and they preach'd Damnation to him, if he refus'd to let Christ have his Spouse.
Eu. O the Villany of Fools! But what then?
Ca. I was kept close at Home for three Days; but in the mean Time there were always with me some Women of the College that they call Convertites, mightily encouraging me to persist in my holy Resolution, and watching me narrowly, lest any of my Friends or Kindred should come at me, and make me alter my Mind. In the mean While, my Habit was making ready, and the Provision for the Feast.
Eu. How did you find yourself? Did not your Mind misgive you yet?
Ca. No, not at all; and yet I was so horridly frighted, that I had rather die ten Times over, than suffer the same again.
Eu. What was that, pray?
Ca. It is not to be uttered.
Eu. Come, tell me freely, you know I'm your Friend.
Ca. Will you keep Counsel?
Eu. I should do that without promising, and I hope you know me better than to doubt of it.

VIRGIN

EUPHEMIUS: What birds do I see here?
CATHARINA: That is the patriarch of the college. Do not withdraw; they have already finished drinking. Sit with me for a little while, and once he has departed, we shall converse in our usual manner.
EUPHEMIUS: Come now, I will entreat you for what you previously refused me. Now that we are alone, tell me the whole story, for I would prefer to learn it from you.
CATHARINA: Of all the many friends whom I thought I valued most, I now realize there was no one who gave me more prudent or mature advice than you, the youngest of them all.
EUPHEMIUS: But how did you overcome the affection of your parents?
CATHARINA: First, it was through the wicked urgings of monks and nuns. Then, my mother’s spirit was swayed by my own prayers and entreaties. My father could not be persuaded by any means. Finally, after all possible devices were employed, he was defeated and overwhelmed rather than truly consenting. It happened while they were drinking; they threatened a horrible and ruinous end if he refused his daughter to Christ.
EUPHEMIUS: O, the wickedness of these fools! What happened next?
CATHARINA: I was kept hidden at home for three days. In the meantime, several women from that college, whom they call <term>Conversae</term> <gloss>lay sisters or converts</gloss>, were always present. They added courage with their exhortations, urging me to persist in my holy purpose, and they carefully guarded against any of my female relatives or friends approaching me, for fear they might seem to change my mind. Meanwhile, my garments and other things pertaining to the celebration were being prepared.
EUPHEMIUS: What was your state of mind during this time? Did you waver?
CATHARINA: No, but I suffered something so horrific that I would rather die ten times over than endure it again.
EUPHEMIUS: I beg you, what was that?
CATHARINA: I cannot speak of it.
EUPHEMIUS: What you tell me, you tell to your friend.
CATHARINA: Do you promise silence?
EUPHEMIUS: I would have guaranteed that even if you had not stipulated it. As if you did not know me yet.

<summary>Catharina recounts to Euphemius the intense psychological and social pressure she endured from monks, nuns, and her own parents to force her into religious life, mentioning an traumatic secret event she cannot yet voice.</summary>

[context] Afterward We administer it with the same Preparation, and the same Projection, pouring it upon the Substance of Luna. And yet thence results not a
splendid bright Colour, but dull and livid, with a mortiferous Citrinity.
But the way of colouring it, which is made by Vitriol, or Copperas, is thus: ℞ of either of them a certain Quantity, and sublime as much thereof, as can be sublimed, until with great expression of Fire it be sublimed. After this again sublime this Sublimate with Fire appropriate to it, that of it part after part may be fixed, until its greater part is fixed. But afterward, it must be warily calcined, that a greater Fire may be administred for its Perfection. This being done, it is dissolved into a most Red Water, that hath not its Peer. Then so operate, as you may give it Ingress into the Lunar Body. These Processes are sufficiently demonstrated to you, if you be a true Searcher of the perfect Work, as We have described it. For We, seeing things of this kind profoundly and amicably to adhere to Luna, have considered (and it is certain) that these are from its own Radix; and thence it is, that Luna is altered by them. These Medicines, which We have here inferred, are all of the first Order. Yet there may be manifold other Methods of these Medicines, salving the Essence of Pigmental Things, in the Variety of Methods. [For the Medicine of Argentvive is not in this first Order, seeing it is not a Medicine altering Luna with one only Difference, but altogether in total Compleatment.] Others have invented many Medicines, yet one of these two necessarily happens, viz. either they are constrained to create the Medicine of the same Things, or of Things having the same Nature; or else they compound a Medicine, which with its Alteration is equivalent to that, which it is not, and which neither confers to the Clean, nor to the Parts of the Clean, until the Mover, in the sublime Mobile of Nature, rests uncorrupt.

Indeed, the Moon <note>alchemical term for silver</note> is also citrinated with the dissolution of Mars <note>alchemical term for iron</note>.
The method of that citrination which is perfected by <term>Vitriol</term> <gloss>a sulfate mineral</gloss> or <term>Cuperosa</term> <gloss>copper sulfate/vitriol</gloss> is as follows. Let a certain quantity of each of these be taken, and let that part which is capable of sublimation be sublimed until it is sublimed with total expression. After this, let what has been sublimed be sublimed again with the appropriate degree of fire, so that something from it is fixed after something else, until the greater part of it is fixed. Afterwards, let it be administered with the caution of fire, so that a greater fire may be administered to it for perfection. After this, let it be dissolved into a most ruby-red water, to which there is no equal. Then, you shall devise a way to provide it with entry into the Lunar body <note>the body of silver</note>, and these devices have been sufficiently shown to you if you are an inquirer of the perfect work which we have written. And because we see that things of this kind adhere amicably to the depth of the Moon, we have considered—and it is certain—that these are of their root, and therefore it happens that they are altered through them. These are indeed all the medicines of the first order which we have brought forth; however, many methods of them can be multiplied, provided the essence of the pigmentary substances is maintained in the variety of the methods. Some, indeed, have discovered more medicines, but it necessarily happens that one of two things occurs: either it is necessary for them to create medicine from the same things or from things having the same nature, or they compose a medicine which is equivalent to what is not, along with its alteration, and which confers nothing to the world, nor to the parts of the world, until the mover in the sublime, mobile nature has rested uncorrupted.

[context] not only for the sake of the uses and fruits of the practice, but from impatience to obtain in the shape of some new work an assurance for themselves
that it is worth their while to go on; and also to show themselves off to the world, and so raise the credit of the business in which they are engaged. Thus, like Atalanta, they go aside to pick up the golden apple, but meanwhile they interrupt their course, and let the victory escape them. But in the true course of experience, and in carrying it on to the effecting of new works, the divine wisdom and order must be our pattern. Now God on the first day of creation created light only, giving to that work an entire day, in which no material substance was created. So must we likewise from experience of every kind first endeavour to discover true causes and axioms; and seek for experiments of Light, not for experiments of Fruit. For axioms rightly discovered and established supply practice with its instruments, not one by one, but in clusters, and draw after them trains and troops of works. Of the paths however of experience, which no less than the paths of judgment are impeded and beset, I will speak hereafter; here I have only mentioned ordinary experimental research as a bad kind of demonstration. But now the order of the matter in hand leads me to add something both as to those signs which I lately mentioned,—(signs that the systems of philosophy and contemplation in use are in a bad condition)—and also as to the causes of what seems at first so strange and incredible. For a knowledge of the signs prepares assent; an explanation of the causes removes the marvel: which two things will do much to render the extirpation of Idols from the understanding more easy and gentle.

But concerning the ways of experimenting, which are no less beset and blocked than the ways of judging, we shall speak later: for the present, we have spoken only of common Experience, as if it were a poor Demonstration. Now, the order of things requires that we append something concerning those signs which we mentioned a little earlier (that philosophies and contemplations currently are in a bad state); and concerning the causes of a thing so wonderful and incredible at first glance. For the awareness of the signs prepares the way for assent; but the explanation of the causes removes the miracle. These two things help much toward a more easy and gentle extirpation of Idols from the Intellect.

Stellæ, inquit, omnes rotundæ sunt, Cometæ porrecti, ex quo apparet stellas non esse. Quis em̃ tibi concedet Cometas longos esse, quorum natura quidem ut cæterorū globus est? Cæterum fulgor extenditur quemadmodū sol radios suos longe lateque dimittit. Cæterum ipsi alia est forma, alia ei qui ex ipso fluit lumini. Sic Cometarum corpus ipsum corrotundat̃. Splendor autē longior q̃ cæterorū syderū apparet. Quare inquis: Dic tu mihi prius, quare luna dissimillimū soli lumen accipiat, cū accipiat a sole? Quare modo rubeat, modo palleat? Quare liuidus illi & ater color sit, cū a cōspectu solis excluditur? Dic mihi quare omnes stellæ inter se dissimile habeant aliquatenus faciem, diuersissimā soli. Quomodo nihil prohibet ita sydera esse, quuis similia non sint, ita nihil prohibet Cometas æternos esse & sortis eiusdē, cuius cætera, etiam si faciem illis non habent similē. Quid porro mundus ipse si consyderes illum, nōne ex diuersis cōpositus est? Quid est quare in leone semper sol ardeat, & terras æstibus torreat? in aquario astringat hyemē? flumina gelu claudat? Et hoc tamen & illud sydus eiusdem cōditionis <margin>† exoritur</margin> est, cum effectu & natura dissimile sit. Intra breuissimū tempus aries † excolitur, libra tardissime mergitur, & tamen hoc sydus & illud eiusdem naturæ est, cum illud exiguo tempore ascēdat, hoc diu proferatur. Non uides q̃ contraria inter se elementa sint? grauia & leuia sunt, frigida & calida, humida & sicca. Tota huius mundi concordia ex discordia constat. Negas Cometem stellam esse, quia forma eius non respondeat ad exemplar, nec sit cæteris similis. Vides enim, simillima est illa, quæ tricesimo anno reuertitur ad locum suum, huic quæ intra annum reuisit sedem suam. Nō ad unam natura formam opus suum præstat, sed ipsa uarietate se iactat. Alia morosiora, alia uelociora alijs fecit. Alia ualidiora, alia temperatiora, quædam autem eduxit a turba, ut singula & conspicua procederent, quædam in gregem misit. Ignorat naturæ potentiam, qui illi non putat aliquando licere, nisi quod sæpius facit. Cometas non frequenter ostendit, attribuit illis alium locum, alia tempora, dissimiles cæteris motus. Voluit ex his magnitudinem operis sui colere, quorum formosior facies est, q̃ ut fortuita putes, siue amplitudinem eorum consyderes, siue fulgorem, qui maior est ardentiorsq̃ q̃ cæteris. Aristoteles ait Cometas significare tempestatem & uentorum intemperantiam atq̃ imbrium. Quid ergo? non iudicas sydus esse, quod futura denunciat? [context] The appearance of slowness in their motion is caused by their encountering the sun, as well as by
the character of their paths and the position of their orbits, which are at certain periods calculated to deceive the eye. Ships in the same way moving under full sail seem withal to be stationary. Men will some day be able to demonstrate in what regions comets have their paths, why their course is so far removed from the other stars, what is their size and constitution. Let us be satisfied with what we have discovered, and leave a little truth for our descendants to find out.

We cannot, Apollonius says, see through the stars what is beyond, but sight passes easily through the comets. Well, in the first place, if that is the case, it is not so in the part of the body which consists of dense solid fire, but only where the dispersed glow extends as it breaks up into the appearance of hair. One can see through the gaps in the fire and not through the fire itself. Stars again, it is said, are all round, comets extended; whence it is plain that they are not true stars. But who, pray, will allow that comets are long? Their tendency like that of other stars is to a globe shape, only the light from them is prolonged. The sun shoots out his rays far and wide, but has himself a shape different from that of the light that streams from him. So in comets, the body is rounded, but the glow from them presents the appearance of being longer than that of the other stars.

WHY is this so, you ask. Do you tell me first why the light the moon receives is wholly unlike the sun although she receives it from the sun. Why is it now ruddy, now pale? why is her colour ashen or black when she is cut off from the sun's view? Or tell me why all the stars have aspects to some extent dissimilar to one another and all as different as possible from the sun. It is no hindrance to their being true stars that they are not all alike; so there is nothing to prevent comets from being permanent through all time, sharing the same destiny as the other stars, even though they have not an appearance like theirs. Besides, is not the universe, if you will only examine it carefully, made up of contrarieties? Why is it that the sun should be always blazing hot in Leo, scorching the ground with his fierce glow, while in Aquarius he brings winter's chain and closes the rivers with ice? The one constellation is subject to the same law as the other, though its characteristics and influence are so different. Aries again rises in a moment, Libra lifts its scales very slowly; yet the one sign is of the same nature as the other, though that one mounts in a brief space, this comes forth very deliberately. Do you not see, too, how contrary the elements are to one another? They are heavy and light, cold and hot, moist and dry. The whole concord of the universe is a harmony of discords. You say a comet is not a star, because its form does not correspond to the type,
[context] but is unlike other stars.

Quod per illa verba significetur ex Naturali & Sensuali Divino, est sensus superior ; quae enim inferiora Ecclesiae sunt, illa dicuntur esse ex Naturali & Sensuali Divino Domini, non quod in Domino haec sint inferiora, nam in Domino & in Ipsius Divino Humano omne est Infinitum, est enim Jehovah quoad utramque Essentiam n : 2156. 2329. 2921. 3023 ; sed quia ita est apud hominem ; qui enim sensuales homines sunt, sensualiter capiunt illa quae in Domino sunt & quae ex Domino, & qui naturales naturaliter ; ex qualitate illorum qui recipiunt, ita dicitur ; qui autem coelestes homines sunt, & inde vere rationales, illi interiora percipiunt, de illis dicitur quod doceantur ex Rationali Divino Domini ; hic est sensus superior, ut dictum, qui per illa verba significatur. Quod vallis sint inferiora Ecclesiae, constare potest ab aliis locis in Verbo ; ut apud Esaiam *“ Propheticum vallis visionis ; quid tibi hic, quod adscendisti omnis in tecta : dies tumultus, & conculcationis, & perplexitatis Domino Jehovih Zebaoth, in Valle visionis,”* XXII : 1. 5 ; vallis visionis pro phantasiis de spiritualibus ex sensualibus, ita ex inferioribus. Apud Eundem *“ Selectio vallium tuarum impletae sunt curru, & equites ponendo posuerunt ad portam,”* XXII : 7 ; electio vallium pro bonis & veris in naturali seu externo homine. Apud Eundem *“ Vox clamantis in deserto, parate viam Jehovae, complanate in solitudine semitam Deo nostro, omnis vallis extolletur,”* XL : 3. 4 ; vallis pro humilibus. Apud Jeremiam,

It is said, every coming, when truth from the Word flows into the thought.
4713. "And the peace of the flock."—That hereby is signified how the case was with those who learnt, or the church, appears (1.) from the signification of peace, as denoting how the case was, see above, n. 4712; and (2.) from the signification of flock, as denoting those who learn: for the shepherd, or he who feeds, is one who teaches and leads to the good of charity; and the flock is he who learns and is led, see n. 343, thus it is the church likewise.
4714. "And bring me word again."—That hereby is signified knowledge, appears from the signification of bringing word again, as denoting to relate how the case was, thus denoting knowledge.
4715. "And he sent him from the valley of Hebron."—That hereby is signified from the Divine Natural and Sensual principle, appears (1.) from the signification of being sent, as denoting to proceed and teach, see above, n. 4710; (2.) from the signification of valley, as denoting those things which are beneath, see n. 1723, 3417; and (3.) from the signification of Hebron, as denoting the Lord's church as to good, see n. 2909. Thus by the above words is signified that he taught those things of the church which are inferior, and this because they did not comprehend superior things; for he who teaches faith and not charity, cannot possibly perceive the superior or interior things of the church, since he has not any thing which guides and dictates whether this be of faith, or true; but if he teaches charity, he then has good, which is to him a dictate, and guides him, for all truth is from and treats of good, or, what is the same thing, the all of faith is from and treats of charity; every one may know from mere natural light, that the all of doctrine has respect to life. That by the above words is signified from the Divine Natural and Sensual principle, is a superior sense; for the inferior things of the church are said to be from the Lord's Divine Natural and Sensual principle; not that these things are inferior in the Lord, for in Him and in His Divine Human principle all is infinite, inasmuch as He is Jehovah as to each essence, n. 2156, 2329, 2921, 3023, but because it is so with man. For they who are sensual men, have a sensual apprehension of those things which are in and from the Lord, and they who are natural have a natural apprehension; the above form of expression is used, owing to the quality of those who receive the Word. But they who are celestial men, and thence truly rational, have a perception of interior things; and it is said of them, that they are taught from the Lord's Divine Rational principle; this is the superior sense, as was said, which is signified by the above words. That a valley denotes the inferior things of the church, may appear from other passages in the Word, as in Isaiah, "The prophecy of the valley of vision. What aileth thee here, that thou hast wholly gone up to the tops of the houses? . . . A day of tumult, and of treading under foot, and of perplexity by the Lord Jehovah Zebaoth, in the valley of vision" xxii. 1, 5; the valley of vision denotes phantasies concerning spiritual things arising from sensual principles, thus from lower things. Again, in the same prophet, "The choice of thy valleys have been filled with chariots, and horsemen have set themselves in array at the gate," xxii. 7; the choice of valleys denotes goods and truths in the natural or external man. Again, "The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of Jehovah, make plain in the desert a highway for our God; every valley shall be exalted," xl. 3, 4; where valley denotes the lowly.
